newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Russia sales fall to help platinum - Amplats.
newsitem.headline: Russia sales fall to help platinum - Amplats.

text.p: Platinum and gold prices will delink once Russian sales decline and the fundamentals of the two metals reassert themselves, Anglo American Platinum Corp (Amplats) chairman Barry Davison said on Monday.
Reiterating comments made last week, Davison told a news conference he believed the main reason for the fall in platinum and gold was the high level of liquidity in both markets.

"Clearly platinum has been tracking gold and the reason it has been tracking gold is because there is plenty of liquidity in the gold market and there is certainly plenty of liquidity in the platinum...market."
Platinum traditionally trades at a premium to gold but has recently moved in line with it.

Russia, the world's second largest producer of platinum, is known to have sold platinum, palladium and gold well above planned sales levels in 1995 and 1996, although the size of its stockpiles remains a closely guarded state secret.
Analysts have previously estimated Russian platinum stockpiles at between two million and five million ounces.
Davison said that in the medium term, as a decline in Russian sales drained liquidity from the market, the prices of gold and platinum would begin to decouple.

"The market at some stage is going to become aware of a significantly reduced level of sales from Russia. The timing is difficult but it is going to happen as the Russian stocks get lower and lower," he said.
At that stage, the fundamental differences in the basics of supply and demand for platinum and gold would begin to exert themselves and would be shown in the prices, Davison said.

"In the last nine years since I have been involved in this business the highest premium to gold has been around $130. That demonstrates that the fundamentals for platinum are different from gold. The price is capable of delinking itself and moving in a different direction," he added.
In the short term, however, Davison expected precious metal prices to continue to waste away, bringing further pressure to bear on the company's earnings.
The company earlier announced a 28.5 percent fall in earnings to 53.9 cents a share for the six months to December 31.
It blamed the poor performance on weak precious metal prices, higher working costs and a strike at its Rustenburg Platinum Holdings Ltd mine last June which cost the company around 250 million rand.
"The outlook for the second half of the year is really not good," he said.

"We will do what we can whatever we can to mitigate the ongoing rise in costs and the weaker revenues to try and improve the results in the second half year but quite clearly it is going to be extraordinarily difficult," Davison said.
South Africa produces 76 percent of the world's newly-mined platinum, of which about half comes from Amplats mines in the country's North West and Northern provinces.
Platinum closed at $351.00/352.00 in London on Monday -- a $5 premium to the gold price which ended at $346.05/55 an ounce.
